Magnetic flux is the same as the magnetic field strength.
A magnetic field parallel to a surface produces maximum magnetic flux through it.
Magnetic flux is a vector because the magnetic field is a vector.
Gauss’ law for magnetism says the magnetic field is zero everywhere.
A magnetic field has no flux through a closed surface because magnetic fields do not cross surfaces.
A single north or south magnetic pole can exist independently.
An induced electromotive force occurs only when the circuit is closed and current flows.
A magnetic field must change in strength for an electromotive force to be induced.
Any motion of a conductor through a magnetic field produces an induced electromotive force.
The induced current always opposes the external magnetic field.
The induced emf always produces a current in the opposite direction to the changing current.
If the magnetic flux is large, the induced emf must be large.
A faster change in magnetic flux always transfers more total charge.
No charge is transferred if the magnetic flux changes back to its original value.
The total transferred charge is determined only by the magnetic flux change and is independent of circuit resistance.
Motional emf is produced only when the magnetic field changes with time.
Any motion of a conductor through a magnetic field produces motional emf.
The entire conductor must form a closed circuit for motional emf to exist.
A rotating coil produces emf simply because it is moving.
The induced emf is greatest when the magnetic flux is greatest.
The magnetic field must change for emf to be induced.
Self-inductance is the magnetic flux produced by the coil.
A coil has self-induced emf whenever a current flows through it.
Self-inductance depends only on the current in the coil.
Self-inductance increases only linearly with the number of turns.
A larger coil always has a smaller self-inductance because the turns are farther apart.
Self-inductance is determined by the coil's resistance or by the current flowing through it.
An inductor stores electrical charge like a capacitor.
An inductor stores energy only when the current is increasing.
An inductor immediately releases all its stored energy when the circuit is opened.
The current reaches its final value immediately when the switch is closed.
The inductor prevents current from flowing permanently.
The current increases at a constant rate.
The current becomes zero immediately when the source is switched off.
The current decreases linearly with time.
The inductor continues to supply constant current after switching off.
Mutual induction occurs only when the two circuits are physically connected.
A steady current in the first circuit continuously induces an emf in the second circuit.
The induced current in the second circuit flows in the same direction as the current change in the first circuit.
Mutual inductance is simply the sum of the two coils’ self-inductances.
The coefficient of coupling is always 1 for coupled coils.
Mutual inductance depends only on the physical separation of the coils.
The inductances cancel because the coils are separate and do not share magnetic flux.
Different currents flow through the two inductors because they have different inductance values.
The equivalent inductance depends on whether the coils are wound in the same or opposite direction.
The equivalent inductance of parallel uncoupled inductors is the sum of their inductances.
The current through each parallel inductor is always equal.
Parallel inductors must have mutual coupling between them.
Alternating current always has a constant magnitude and only changes direction.
The current reverses direction every cycle, so one complete cycle contains only one reversal.
The average value of a sinusoidal alternating current over a complete cycle is its peak value.
The RMS value is the arithmetic average of the instantaneous current or voltage values.
The RMS value is equal to the peak value.
An AC supply with zero average voltage has no heating or power effect.
The average value of an alternating current over a complete cycle is equal to its peak value divided by two.
The average value is the same as the RMS value.
The average value is found by averaging only the positive peak and negative peak values.
The current and voltage are always constant in a purely resistive AC circuit.
Current leads or lags voltage in a purely resistive AC circuit.
Resistance changes the phase relationship between AC voltage and current.
The current leads the voltage by 90 degrees in a purely inductive circuit.
The current and voltage are in phase because the circuit is supplied by AC voltage.
The inductor consumes average real power like a resistor.
The current lags the voltage by 90 degrees in a purely capacitive circuit.
The current and voltage are in phase because the circuit is connected to an AC source.
A capacitor continuously consumes real power like a resistor.
The impedance is found by simply adding resistance and inductive reactance as ordinary numbers.
An ideal inductor has the same opposition to current at every frequency.
The current and source voltage are in phase because the resistor and inductor are connected in series.
Average power is always equal to the product of rms voltage and rms current.
The inductor consumes real power continuously like the resistor.
Power factor is the ratio of rms current to rms voltage.
Resistance and capacitive reactance are added directly to find impedance.
The impedance of a series R-C circuit is always greater than R + Xc.
Capacitive reactance increases as AC frequency increases.
Impedance is simply the sum of resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.
Inductive and capacitive reactance always increase the circuit's impedance.
Impedance is measured only in ohms of resistance and has no phase-related component.
Current is always in phase with the applied voltage in an AC circuit.
A circuit is inductive whenever it contains an inductor, regardless of its capacitors.
Greater capacitive reactance makes current lead voltage more strongly.
At series resonance, the circuit impedance is zero.
Resonance occurs when the inductance equals the capacitance.
The voltage across each reactive component must be zero at resonance.
The Q-factor is the voltage across the inductor or capacitor at all frequencies.
A higher Q-factor means a larger applied voltage.
The Q-factor is always equal to the voltage across both the inductor and capacitor added together.
A transformer can operate normally with direct current.
A transformer creates additional electrical energy.
The primary and secondary coils are electrically connected.
The voltage ratio equals the inverse turns ratio.
An ideal transformer produces more electrical power when it increases voltage.
An ideal transformer can have an efficiency greater than 100%.
A transformer produces power from nothing because it changes voltage and current.
Transformer efficiency is the ratio of secondary voltage to primary voltage.
